findings.finding: Gold agreement is to be computed with the `parity.verdict_decision` mapping. That helper was written for per-criterion `run_case` outputs and maps `verdict == "FAIL"` OR any non-empty `findings` to `block`. The plan_review_verdict contract uses PASS/BLOCK/INDETERMINATE, never FAIL, and carries advisory findings. Applied to it, the helper would call every PASS-with-advisories review a `block`, and decide BLOCK verdicts only by whether findings are present. This is a cargo-cult reuse: the helper is borrowed for its name without checking what it maps.

findings.finding: The plan treats a case's gold label as the right answer for a whole-ticket review, but the labels are per criterion. In `eligible_cases`, `expect: pass`/`finding` comes from a single-criterion eval case (e.g. `criterion: T10`), and `GOLD_EXPECTS` turns it into block/advisory. A gold-`pass` T10 case only asserts that no T10 finding should fire. A full review can still BLOCK correctly on another criterion, and a gold-`finding` case's defect may surface as advisory. Container cases are also eligible only because they carry `children` (`_runnable`). The harness creates a single task ticket from `input` alone and drops those children, so those cases get reviewed as leaves against labels set for a decomposition.

findings.finding: The gold labels are criterion-scoped: `expect: finding|pass` says whether ONE criterion's finder should fire on the fragment. The harness compares them with a WHOLE-review BLOCK/non-BLOCK decision, which is a proxy. A gold-'pass' case can legitimately BLOCK on any other criterion. A gold-'finding' case can legitimately surface its finding as advisory only: in the pipeline the decision depends on priority against block_threshold, and in the agent only `blocker` severity blocks. Per-engine gold agreement then measures how often an unrelated whole-review outcome happens to line up with a single-criterion label, not engine quality.
scenarios: A T10 'pass' fragment BLOCKs on G6/T2 under both engines: both are scored as gold disagreements even though both may be right.
A T10 'finding' case surfaces a major T10 advisory under the agent (not a blocker): scored as a miss.

findings.finding: The greedy one-to-one Jaccard matching does not specify the greedy order. A different traversal order (pipeline-finding order vs highest-similarity-first) yields different matched counts, so the overlap metric and its test expectations are underdetermined.

findings.suggested_fix: Score every (pipeline, agentic) finding pair. Sort the pairs by Jaccard descending, breaking ties by index. Accept a pair when both members are still unmatched and its score ≥ MATCH_THRESHOLD.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the overlap similarity robust to length asymmetry (e.g. match on the agent's title, or use an overlap coefficient |A∩B|/min(|A|,|B|)) and include a worked test with an asymmetric-length same-defect pair.
evidence: agentic_verdict.map_finding: `text = f"{title}: {description}"`
sidecar._norm_tokens keeps every token longer than 3 characters, so a long description contributes many unshared tokens
findings.finding: Token-set Jaccard ≥ 0.5 penalizes length asymmetry. The agentic engine's finding text is `title: description` (map_finding concatenates both), while a pipeline finding is a single claim sentence. When the same defect is described at those two lengths, the union is dominated by the longer text and Jaccard falls below 0.5 even if the shorter set is nearly contained in the longer one. Overlap is then biased toward 'pipeline-only'/'agentic-only'.
findings.location: Approach → Report → finding overlap ('token-set Jaccard similarity ≥ MATCH_THRESHOLD = 0.5')
scenarios: Pipeline: 'Gold mapping always returns advisory for BLOCK verdicts' vs agent: a title plus a three-sentence description of the same bug. Most of the pipeline tokens are contained in the agent text, but Jaccard is about 0.3, so the pair is unmatched.

findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) drop `--limit 6` from the recorded run, run the full filtered stratified corpus, update the wall-time estimate, and record `corpus_digest` over exactly the items run; or (b) if a full run is too costly in wall time, first update the parent epic's AC to allow a sampled run (which stales and re-reviews the parent), and make the sample stratified across specs (e.g. one case per plan-review spec) rather than a `[:6]` prefix of the sorted list. Record both the run-set digest and the full-corpus size in engine_comparison_results.json.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Record each candidate pair's Jaccard score (or the best score per finding) in the per-item results, so the 0.5 threshold can be checked and re-applied after the live run without re-running the models.
evidence: "the two engines word findings differently"
"`MATCH_THRESHOLD = 0.5`, a module constant recorded in the results, not a config key"
"a worked example with 2 near-identical finding texts"
findings.finding: MATCH_THRESHOLD = 0.5 is asserted rather than derived. The tests only check a synthetic 'near-identical' pair and one below-threshold pair, so nothing shows that 0.5 separates same-issue from different-issue findings on real engine output, whose wording the plan says differs.
findings.location: Approach > Report > finding overlap; Testing > Overlap
scenarios: Real paraphrased findings about the same issue score around 0.3, so overlap is reported as near zero and the engines look disjoint.
findings.suggested_fix: Store each finding's normalized token set, plus the best cross-engine Jaccard score and its partner, in the per-item records. Then a later threshold change can be recomputed offline from engine_comparison_results.json.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Report Cohen's kappa (reusing `rebar.llm.evals.eval.cohens_kappa` or tier1's undefined-safe `_cohen_kappa`) alongside the raw verdict-agreement rate, and pin it in test_engine_comparison.py.
evidence: src/rebar/llm/evals/eval.py:343 — `def cohens_kappa(rater_a: list, rater_b: list) -> float`
src/rebar/llm/evals/plan_replay/tier1.py:179-194 — 'per-question agreement (kappa + raw agreement, no-answer excluded)'

Retrieved: python-fiddle.com/tutorials/cohens-kappa — 'Cohen's kappa corrects for this: it subtracts expected chance agreement from observed agreement'; dev.to (techlogstack) — 'Cohen's Kappa — a statistical measure of agreement between two raters that corrects for chance agreement'
findings.finding: Verdict agreement is reported only as a raw match rate plus the confusion matrix. The repo already has chance-corrected agreement for exactly this two-rater comparison (eval.cohens_kappa; plan_replay/tier1._cohen_kappa, which reports raw agreement and kappa side by side). Standard practice for comparing two LLM judges is to report Cohen's kappa alongside raw agreement, because raw agreement is inflated when one label dominates. With roughly 6 items that are mostly PASS or mostly BLOCK, raw agreement alone can look high even if the engines agree only by chance.
findings.location: Approach → Report → 'verdict agreement: the exact PASS/BLOCK/INDETERMINATE match rate'
scenarios: Both engines PASS 5 of 6 items: raw agreement is 0.83, but kappa may be about 0 or undefined, which shows the agreement carries little information.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a `kappa` field next to `agreement` in the report, computed over the same both-ran item pairs with the existing tier1-style helper (None when fewer than 2 pairs or when expected chance agreement equals 1).
